questions.stem: A match does not burst into flames on its own, but does when struck against the matchbox. How does this relate to activation energy?

options.text: Striking provides the oxygen needed for combustion
Striking provides the activation energy needed to start the exothermic combustion reaction
The matchbox contains a catalyst that starts the reaction
Striking changes the match from an endothermic to an exothermic reaction

questions.explanation: The friction from striking the match provides enough energy (as heat) to overcome the activation energy barrier for combustion. Once started, the exothermic combustion reaction is self-sustaining - the energy released by the reaction provides the activation energy for further molecules to react. Without the initial strike, the activation energy barrier prevents the reaction.

questions.stem: A reaction profile shows reactants at 100 kJ, a peak at 250 kJ, and products at 60 kJ. What is the activation energy for the forward reaction?

options.text: 40 kJ
190 kJ
150 kJ
250 kJ

questions.explanation: Activation energy is the difference between the energy of the reactants and the peak of the energy barrier. Ea = 250 - 100 = 150 kJ. Note: 40 kJ is the enthalpy change (100 - 60 = 40), and 190 kJ would be the activation energy for the reverse reaction (250 - 60).

questions.stem: Hydrogen and oxygen gases can be mixed together at room temperature without reacting. However, a small spark causes an explosive reaction. What role does the spark play?

options.text: It acts as a catalyst, lowering the activation energy
It provides the activation energy so some molecules can react, then the exothermic reaction sustains itself
It converts the oxygen into a more reactive form
It increases the pressure of the gases

questions.explanation: At room temperature, the hydrogen and oxygen molecules do not have enough energy to overcome the activation energy barrier. The spark provides enough energy for some molecules to react. Since the reaction (2H2 + O2 -> 2H2O) is highly exothermic, the energy released causes surrounding molecules to react too, creating a chain reaction that appears explosive.

questions.stem: A catalyst lowers the activation energy of a reaction from 120 kJ/mol to 60 kJ/mol. What effect does this have on the enthalpy change of the reaction?

options.text: The enthalpy change is halved
The enthalpy change becomes more negative
The enthalpy change remains unchanged
The enthalpy change doubles

questions.explanation: A catalyst provides an alternative pathway with lower activation energy but does NOT change the enthalpy change. The starting energy (reactants) and finishing energy (products) are unchanged, so Delta H remains the same. The catalyst only affects how quickly the reaction reaches the same final energy state.

questions.stem: Why does increasing temperature increase the rate of a reaction, even though it does not change the activation energy?

options.text: Higher temperature lowers the activation energy needed
Higher temperature means more particles have energy greater than or equal to the activation energy
Higher temperature increases the activation energy, making collisions more effective
Higher temperature only makes particles collide more often, not with more energy

questions.explanation: Increasing temperature gives particles more kinetic energy. This means a greater proportion of particles have energy equal to or exceeding the activation energy, leading to more successful collisions. Additionally, particles move faster and collide more frequently. Both effects increase the rate, but the key factor is the increased proportion of particles exceeding Ea.
